An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.

papers.title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
papers.abstract: Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.

papers.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
papers.abstract: Memory determines which large language models (LLMs) an edge device can run and how fast it runs them: capacity limits a 4 GB Jetson Nano, and bandwidth limits an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed weight formats (GPTQ, AWQ, and the GGUF K- and I-quants) spend the same number of bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. We present LazyWeights, which keeps these formats, tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At 1% and 3.5% perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are 5.7-31.4% smaller than the best GGUF format. A bit-exact 0.21 mm^2 ASIC decoder unit (1 GHz, 7 nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to 36% and 38% (54% and 44% with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, LazyWeights needs 58-64% less time and 53-57% less energy per token than the GGUF runtime on the CPU, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6x faster at 3.89 bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput, and the unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

papers.title: Learning the Missing Derivative: Neural Multiple-Scattering Operators for Inverse Volume Rendering
papers.abstract: Reconstructing optically thick media from photographs requires modeling multiple scattering and its response to changes in extinction. Frozen-source tomography discards this derivative; differentiable path tracing estimates it through expensive, noisy sampling. We instead predict the multiple-scattering field with a neural operator and differentiate through it during inverse rendering, while computing transmittance and single scattering directly. A further challenge arises during optimization: an operator that predicts the field accurately on held-out media can still produce poor derivatives at the density states visited by the optimizer. We address this by fine-tuning on states generated during inversions driven by the operator, using Monte Carlo scattering-field supervision. On held-out optically thick clouds, our method improves relighting over frozen-source tomography at equal time and outperforms differentiable path tracing given substantially more time. Training on inversion trajectories also improves derivative alignment at visited states and reduces optimization drift.

papers.title: FRIDA: Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies. I. Programme overview, resolved gas density profiles, and HI mass-size relation
papers.abstract: Gas-rich ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) provide powerful tests of galaxy formation models at low surface densities. However, the structure of their neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) remains poorly constrained, hampering our understanding of this population. We present FRIDA (Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies), a MeerKAT and VLA programme providing high-resolution HI data of 12 gas-rich UDGs. In this paper, we introduce our sample and delve into the associated observations and data reduction. We derive HI fluxes, masses ($M_{\rm HI}$), and resolved surface density profiles ($Σ_{\rm HI}(R)$). We find extended ($\sim 7-30\ \rm{kpc}$ in radius) and regular HI emission in our UDGs, and we report the discovery of a satellite around one of them. Most UDGs in FRIDA have $Σ_{\rm HI}(R)$ profiles with flat inner parts reaching $Σ_{\rm HI}(R)\approx 4\ M_\odot\ \rm{pc^{-2}}$ near their centres, which then decline exponentially in their outer parts. By modelling the HI morphology of the UDGs, we find a median inclination of $43^\circ$, in agreement with theoretical expectations for disc galaxies under UDG selection effects. Moreover, we place our UDGs in the $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm HI}$ and $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm 50,HI}$ mass-size relations, where $R_{\rm HI}$ is radius at which $Σ_{\rm HI}(R)=1\ M_\odot \rm{pc^{-2}}$, and $R_{\rm 50,HI}$ is the radius enclosing $50\%$ of $M_{\rm HI}$. While our UDGs lie within the scatter of the relations, they systematically fall on their upper side, being slightly (by $\sim 15-25\%$) more extended and of lower mean $Σ_{\rm HI}$ (by $\sim 25-35\%$) than average galaxies at similar $M_{\rm HI}$. Moreover, we find that $Σ_{\rm HI}(R/R_{\rm HI})$ and $M_{\rm HI}(<R)/M_{\rm HI}$ for UDGs follow an intermediate trend between late-type discs and early-type galaxies, with a large overlap with Sa galaxies.

papers.title: Another Multivector Inverse Algorithm
papers.abstract: A numerical algorithm is described for computing the inverse of a non-singular multivector across dimensions. The method wraps a reversion-like product around a Faddeev--LeVerrier--Souriau (FLS) polynomial core. While FLS provides dimensional extensibility, the wrapper reduces the polynomial order of the FLS method, and introduces a sparse multivector which can be further exploited. The construction and essential properties of the initial involution are explained. For dimensions 4--7, the optimized inverse requires fewer real multiplications than a same-dimension multivector product. Dimensions 8--11 follow easily on common hardware with similar efficiency. For dimensions 12--15, higher-precision arithmetic demonstrates the generality of the algorithm when the arithmetic can support it. Performance on common hardware is reported. Directions are included for obtaining a Python package with examples for numerical computation in Clifford algebra, supporting arbitrary signatures including degenerate cases.

papers.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
papers.abstract: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.

papers.title: Persistent A-homotopy of Networks: free groups and periodic structures
papers.abstract: We study how loop classes in a network change when cycles up to a prescribed length are declared contractible. The resulting sequence of quotient groups contains the fundamental group of the clique complex at length three and the graph $A$-fundamental group at length four. Its mod-two abelianisation has a barcode whose death scales are the lengths in a minimum cycle basis. This separates the choice of a network filtration from the choice of local loop relations and provides a computable connection between persistent $A$-homotopy and persistent homology. We illustrate the construction on lattices, Watts--Strogatz networks and nine benchmark networks. Filling the plaquettes of a periodic square lattice recovers the fundamental group of the torus. In the Watts--Strogatz simulations, the normalised largest death scale falls below the normalised mean path length over the sampled range, while most clique-homology classes survive the square relations at small rewiring probabilities. The power grid has fewer surviving classes but a longer tail of death scales than five degree-preserving randomisations. We also examine connectivity graphs of maximal cliques in ego networks. Explicit certificates establish non-trivial $A$-classes even though the original ego clique complexes are contractible. The group construction and its linear summary answer related but distinct questions about which loop relations a network model permit.

papers.title: Limitations of Interpretations in Semiring Semantics
papers.abstract: Interpretations have been widely used in the study of provenance of queries on semiring-annotated databases. Here, we consider two different interpretation-based semantics for first-order formulas in negation normal form, namely, the canonical-interpretation semantics and the compatible-interpretation semantics. We show that the resulting query languages cannot express the monus operation on semiring-annotated relations, when the annotations come from a positive semiring with monus and with at least three elements in its universe. Consequently, the semantics of SQL cannot be captured using the interpretation-based semantics considered here.

papers.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, the standard injection template (AgentDojo's important_instructions) never redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY. Across 12 AgentDojo cells, SPILLWAY leads tested defenses in mean under-attack utility and composite scores. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, mean attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker stays below one percent, and SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

papers.title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $ε$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $ετ$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $ε$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

papers.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
papers.abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $μ$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.

papers.title: Morphological Features of Murine Pulmonary Arterial Networks for Diagnosing Vascular Disease
papers.abstract: Hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension results from prolonged time spent in a low-oxygen environment. The induced pulmonary hypertension leads to vascular remodeling, including vessel dilation and decreased compliance. This study aims to identify changes in vascular morphology in mice with pulmonary hypertension induced by hypoxia. To do so, we examine the pulmonary arterial network morphology using methods from geometry, topological data analysis, and statistical shape analysis. Tools from these fields are applied to arterial networks excised from micro-CT images of thirteen mice at four pressures. Networks from the hypertensive mice were normalized via a radius pruning algorithm, and analysis was conducted on the entire arterial network, as well as on a per-lobe basis. The main objective of this study was to present an adaptable pipeline for extracting features from micro-CT images to study how vascular disease affects arterial network morphology. Using this pipeline, we showed that the hypertensive mice have increased radius ratios and decreased length-to-radius ratios. Persistent homology analysis revealed that hypertension leads to lower branch-to-branch proximity and lower directional complexity in both the posterior and anterior directions. Persistence curves, particularly Betti curves, revealed lobe-specific differences in the left and inferior lobes. The first two shape principal component scores were also able to discriminate between control and hypertension at lower pressures. Importance metrics for each feature are computed using a boosted decision tree, and then an SVM classification model is fit with the most informative predictors for hypertensive classification.

papers.title: HEDGE: Gated Hypergraph Memory for Scalable Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate systems require agents to retain and revisit arguments across multiple rounds, yet limited context windows and unstructured memories make relevant information increasingly difficult to recover. Existing flat and pairwise-graph memories also struggle to capture higher-order relations, including multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus. We introduce HEDGE, a selective memory framework that represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs. Hyperedges connect related claims across agents, while intra-hyperedge relational graphs preserve fine-grained argumentative structure. A learned memory selection module (MSM), trained through supervised learning and reinforcement learning, routes each memory candidate to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT, retaining useful information while limiting redundancy. Across seven diverse benchmarks, HEDGE consistently outperforms strong single-agent, multi-agent, and memory baselines, improving accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent system with GPT-4o-mini. The gains reach 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while HEDGE reduces memory usage by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%. Code is available at: https://github.com/AmirAbaskohi/HEDGE.

papers.title: Morse-Maxwell Theory for Directed Acyclic Graph
papers.abstract: The Maxwell graph of a directed acyclic graph records the extrema of its iterated basin and hill boundaries. Their unweighted counts need not satisfy Morse inequalities, and the reduction can change homology. We assign multiplicities using the reduced homology of lower and upper order links and retain every vertex with nonzero local homology. This modified reduction preserves both hierarchies, the local groups, and the homology of all sublevel and superlevel order complexes. Its Morse numbers satisfy the weak and strong Morse inequalities over any field. We give explicit formulas in low dimensions and for complete layered graphs. We also construct local Morse numbers for path homology and prove agreement with the reachability construction on complete layered graphs, including those without transitive arrows. Counterexamples distinguish the homology theories and show that local Morse degrees need not equal vertex depths. A comparison with discrete-gradient methods explains the role of auxiliary choices.

papers.title: What the Trace Shows and What the Label Says: Auditing Behavioral Detectors in Agent Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, yet evaluations rarely report whether a measurement actually fits the trace it describes. We study what happens when those measurements do not fully capture the trace's behavior. Agents solve GSM8K problems with a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, which gives ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported; a chemistry task with search and retrieval tests the case where the model cannot recompute the tool's output. Across eight models and up to 1,000 traces per model, final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation disagree in systematic ways. The most common gap is the silent tool-output override: the model replaces a corrupted value without calling the tool again, so the error stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review finds verification labels the least reliable (\k{appa} =0.29), and checking depends on the task: the same calculator that several models re-checked on arithmetic was never re-checked on chemistry. Execution limits and serving failures also change what is measured. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should be reported with its evidence, whether the detector's question applied, whether the run was censored, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.

papers.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
papers.abstract: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.01 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.

papers.title: Foresight-dependent entropy production in stochastic two-agent dynamics
papers.abstract: Nonreciprocal interactions can break detailed balance by sustaining stationary probability currents. We ask whether such currents can also emerge when agents' immediate coordination preferences are reciprocal but their adjustment rules result from forward-looking optimization. We study a minimal stochastic linear--quadratic game in which two agents control noisy scalar states and minimize individual discounted costs in a full-information feedback Nash equilibrium. The optimized controls yield an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process whose stationary current, entropy production, and inter-agent information flow follow exactly from the Nash feedback. For reciprocal coordination with unequal self-anchoring, the drift asymmetry first appears at order $τ^5$, where $τ$ is the planning timescale, and the normalized entropy production scales as $τ^8$. We trace this delay to one mechanism: the asymmetry is set by the mismatch between the agents' value-function curvatures along the coordinate each does not control. At leading order this equals the mismatch of the corresponding cost curvatures, which instantaneous incentives cannot see and which the coordination cost fixes to zero; unequal persistence of the partners' fluctuations generates a value-function mismatch at order $τ^3$, postponing the asymmetry to fifth order, while a direct stake in the partner's state restores a cubic law. The normalized information flow, of order $τ^4$, identifies the weakly anchored agent as the one that tracks its partner. For conformist--contrarian coupling, normalized entropy production starts from a nonzero limit and initially decreases as $τ^2$; for equal anchoring, we prove that its long-foresight limit lies below the short-foresight value and that the stationary mutual-information flow vanishes. Numerical solutions of the full Nash equations confirm these laws.

papers.title: HEL: A Heterogeneous Extensible Layer for GPU-Resident Runtime Orchestration
papers.abstract: We describe a GPU-resident runtime system, HEL, built on stateful services that persist throughout the lifespan of a user application. A HEL programmer expresses a workload as an application that spawns coroutine-like tasks, which are then scheduled and run by the HEL runtime. HEL supports synchronous and asynchronous tasks, tasks with runtime dependencies, batched task submission, and automatic retries. Applications and tasks run alongside each other on the spatially partitioned GPU. Using producer-consumer and host-RPC benchmarks together with a PFPL compression case study, we show that HEL demonstrates a performance advantage for underutilized GPUs and for scenarios where HEL enables hiding task latency.

papers.title: Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning
papers.abstract: Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-reliance freshness, scoped propagation of evidence changes, decision states, evidence domains (AML, sanctions, PEP, background, identity, and licensing), the U.S. and FATF regulatory context as of August 2026, privacy and disclosure controls, and residual risks.

papers.title: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
papers.abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

papers.title: Conditional limit theorems for open intermittent dynamical systems
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study conditional limit theorems for open intermittent systems endowed with big/small holes. The initial measure for the system can be a class of (non)invariant probability, including the Lebesgue measure. Unlike the limit theorems for closed systems, we obtain an unexpected new limit distribution, which is not a stable law, for both "regular" and singular observables.

papers.title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower-resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross-lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five-language NF4-supervised directions successfully transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama-3.1-8B by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool-calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.

papers.title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
papers.abstract: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor $ν= 3/2$. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension $\sqrt{2}$, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.

papers.title: QuasiStim: Scalable Accurate Non-Pauli Noise Simulation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computer design relies on simulating noisy quantum error correction (QEC) circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large circuit depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators, such as Stim, are the de facto tools for this regime. However, these simulators typically support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. As a result, more realistic device noise models, such as coherent control errors and thermal relaxation, are often approximated using Pauli twirling. This replacement offers speed but can introduce substantial inaccuracies. To address this, we propose QuasiStim for scalable, accurate QEC simulation of realistic noise, with QuasiFold as a compiler frontend and DeltaFrame as a sampling backend. QuasiFold lowers sampling overhead by opportunistically merging non-Pauli noise sites in the quantum circuit without changing the circuit output. DeltaFrame samples the resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating the full tableau for each shot. In our evaluation, QuasiFold can reduce the number of shots by over $1000\times$ on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes under coherent $R_{ZZ}$ noise. Compared to a per-shot tableau simulator, DeltaFrame is $190\times$ to $1479\times$ faster on rotated surface-code memory as $d$ grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also makes the PTA bias measurable: the gap is non-trivial and varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule.

papers.title: Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization: Unified Learning from Offline Demonstrations and On- and Off-Policy Rollouts via a Shared Regression Target
papers.abstract: Reasoning post-training draws on offline demonstrations and policy-generated rollouts, yet conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) separates their objectives and limits continued reuse of collected responses. We propose \textbf{Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization} (CBPO), which makes these sources compatible with one regression loss through a fixed-reference target. Because the generating policy does not enter this target, positive and negative offline completions, reference responses, and current and historical rollouts can share a common reward-labeled record format and replay buffer. As new responses enter the buffer, optimization retains the same regression objective without coordinating separate SFT and RL objectives or requiring stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic. Restricting the available sources gives offline, on-policy, and off-policy variants, while CBPO-Unified combines them. Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO delivers leading \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} performance across benchmarks and data regimes. On Qwen3-1.7B, CBPO-Unified improves benchmark-averaged \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} over SFT DAPO by 2.33 and 4.44 percentage points, respectively. In the replay ablation, retaining historical rollouts improves these metrics by 1.87 and 3.72 percentage points over the no-history configuration.

papers.title: Prompts versus Rules: Auditing and Controlling Speech Naturalness Behaviors in Voice User Simulators
papers.abstract: As voice agents gain more popularity commercially, the user simulators used to evaluate the deployed agents are also being developed to include more realistic, variable, and diverse speech naturalness behaviors -- disfluency, interruption and backchanneling. The quality of the user simulator directly affects the validity of agent evaluation results. However, we find that most studies so far have not examined in detail whether the intended configuration for these behaviors is realized in the simulation. In this study, we audit the realized naturalness behaviors of tau-Voice, our own LLM-based prompting approach across three models, and our rule-based injection algorithm for disfluency, interruption, and backchanneling. We find that prompting for these behaviors is unreliable and produces speech inconsistent with the instructions, placed and distributed less naturally than the instruction implies. In contrast, our rule-based, model-free algorithm produces controllable and diverse naturalness behaviors more aligned with natural speech. Our results suggest that LLMs not purpose-trained for user simulation are not sufficient on their own to represent authentic user behavior, and that linguistically informed deterministic approaches or specialized models are needed to close the gap; auditing and reporting realized naturalness behaviors, rather than configured settings, is what makes that gap visible.

papers.title: StableGrasp: Reconstructing Physically Stable Human Hand Grasps from Single Images
papers.abstract: Reconstructing a physically stable human grasp from a single RGB image is challenging because physically modeling grasps is itself difficult, and the problem requires estimating not only a visually constrained hand pose but also a single static hand control that stabilizes the grasp. Existing methods either model only visual hand geometry without considering physics, or are evaluated with incomplete physical modeling, which limits the physical validity of the resulting grasps. In this paper, we present StableGrasp, a differentiable simulation-based optimization framework that explicitly separates the visual hand pose from a control target that determines the grasping forces. Our method jointly optimizes hand geometry and control by minimizing the kinetic energy of the grasp in a differentiable simulator, while regularizing the hand geometry to preserve visual consistency and geometric plausibility. The reconstructed grasps are substantially more stable under physical simulation with complete physical modeling, while remaining visually consistent with the input images and geometrically plausible. Experiments show that our approach produces far more stable grasps than alternative hand-control strategies, benefiting visual-only grasp reconstruction pipelines by turning their outputs into physically stable grasps.

papers.title: Safeguarding LLMs via Model-Agnostic Latent Safety Signals from Dark Knowledge
papers.abstract: LLMs have advanced rapidly, raising growing concerns about their safety. Recent work has proposed approaches to detect and defend against attacks including defenses at decoding stage that leverage models' hidden states. However, existing decoding-stage defenses suffer from two limitations. First, they introduce a trade-off between safety and over-refusal, where strengthening safety degrades the model's helpfulness on benign queries. Second, many of these methods rely on internal hidden states and are thus restricted to specific architectures, incurring substantial overhead and limited generalization across models. To address these limitations, we introduce LADE (Latent Safety Signals for Defense), which leverages latent safety signals extracted by contrasting harmful and benign queries from dark knowledge (i.e., information carried by the output probability distribution beyond its argmax) in the first-token output probability distribution. Our key insight is that, beyond surface-level refusal tokens, the dark knowledge in the first-token distribution contains latent safety signals, defined as tokens whose probabilities differ sharply between harmful and benign queries. We show that these signals consistently align across LLMs, forming a model-agnostic direction that emerges from safety alignment. LADE consists of three components: (1) Extracting Latent Safety Signals from Dark Knowledge, which selects top-k safety-discriminative tokens from the first-token probability distribution; (2) Tokenizer Mapping, which maps these tokens across different tokenizers to enable model-agnostic application; and (3) kNN-based Discrimination, which classifies queries via a k-Nearest Neighbors search over the mapped tokens. Across diverse LLMs and benchmarks, LADE is robust against a wide range of jailbreak attacks and lowers attack success rates while maintaining a competitive safety-utility trade-off.

papers.title: $\ell$BISG: Probabilistic Race and Ethnicity Prediction Using Group-Specific Name Lists
papers.abstract: Statistically valid estimation of racial and ethnic disparities often requires inferring group membership probabilities from names and geographic locations. The standard method, Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG), requires group frequencies for each name. Such data are available from the U.S. Census Bureau for common names and limited racial categories, but are unavailable for many ethnic groups and rarely exist outside the United States. We propose list-powered BISG ($\ell$BISG), in which we replace these frequencies with group-specific name lists and combine the lists with geographic prevalence data to obtain calibrated group membership probabilities. These lists can be compiled from different sources or generated by large language models (LLMs), despite potentially unknown biases. Under certain conditions on the name lists, $\ell$BISG can also be applied without geographic prevalence data. Empirical validation using U.S. voter files with self-reported race, the full-count 1900 U.S. Census, and the Lebanese voter registry demonstrates that LLM-generated lists yield accurate, well-calibrated probabilities and precise disparity estimates comparable to existing methods that require name-race frequency data. Thus, $\ell$BISG extends probabilistic race and ethnicity prediction to settings where it was previously not thought possible.

papers.title: Bakamjian--Thomas construction and light-front zero modes in pseudoscalar transitions: A comparison with the covariant Bethe--Salpeter model
papers.abstract: We examine the role of light-front zero modes in the extraction of the semileptonic form factor $f_-(q^2)$ between pseudoscalar mesons. In an exactly solvable covariant Bethe--Salpeter (BS) model, we calculate the transverse-current zero-mode contribution directly from the shrinking nonvalence region and reproduce it with an effective operator in the valence convolution. In the valence-only light-front quark model (LFQM) based on the Bakamjian--Thomas (BT) construction, the one-body current is built from on-shell constituent spinors, and the interaction enters through the mass operator and wave functions. The $(+,\perp)$ extraction of $f_-$ is zero-mode free and is saturated by the on-shell overlap. Using the free constituent invariant masses in the internal minus-current projection gives the same $f_-$ from $(+,-)$ after integration. For spacelike momentum transfer, we prove this equality for rotationally invariant radial wave functions with the light-front Jacobian and the adopted pseudoscalar spin coupling, provided the reduced overlaps converge. Subtracting the minus-current result obtained with physical meson masses from the common transverse result gives the BT completion. Current-component independence indirectly identifies this completion as the effective zero-mode contribution missing from the physical-mass minus-current extraction. When the BS valence current and the effective zero-mode operator for the nonvalence endpoint contribution are transferred unchanged to the Gaussian BT-based LFQM, the resulting expression fails to reproduce the component-independent BT result for $f_-$. We construct a mass-weighted complex transverse contour on which the Gaussian wave functions remain analytic for $0<q^2<(m_1+m_2)^2$, where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the initial and final active-quark masses.

papers.title: Kandinsky 6.0 Video: Foundation Models for Synchronized Video and Audio Generation
papers.abstract: We present Kandinsky 6.0 Video, a family of foundation diffusion models for synchronized text-to-audio-video generation, comprising Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite (3B parameters) and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro (29B parameters). Both models generate 5-second video clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio, including lip-sync, in text-to-audio-video (T2AV) and image-to-audio-video (I2AV) modes; a built-in super-resolution model raises the output resolution to Full-HD (1920x1080). Building on the video generation capabilities of Kandinsky 5.0, Kandinsky 6.0 Video employs a dual-stream CrossDiT architecture that connects a pretrained video stream and a newly trained audio stream through bidirectional cross-attention for temporal and semantic alignment. Our continuous pretraining strategy first trains the audio stream from scratch on large-scale audio corpora and then trains both streams jointly on paired audio-video data while preserving unimodal fidelity; pretraining is followed by supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement-learning-based post-training, and distillation. In side-by-side human evaluation, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro clearly outperforms its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and remains competitive with leading audio-video generation models, outperforming LTX 2.5 and Seedance 2.0 in speech quality. To accelerate open research and deployment in multimedia generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.

papers.title: A Missing Piece for Trustworthy AI Reviewers: From Benchmarking Rhetorical Robustness to SciCore Review
papers.abstract: AI reviewers can assign different judgments to manuscripts that report the same science in different wording, potentially rewarding rhetorical optimization over scientific improvement. We formulate Rhetorical Robustness as the joint requirement of stability across content-preserving rewrites and discrimination across papers. We introduce RobustReview, a controlled full-manuscript benchmark with 1,260 manuscript versions, and evaluate 30 reviewer configurations. The benchmark reveals false robustness, where low rewrite sensitivity coincides with score collapse across papers, and shows that human alignment and rhetorical robustness rank reviewers differently. Moreover, the evaluated content-focused prompting protocol does not consistently improve robustness across backbones. Motivated by these findings, we introduce SciCore, a dual-branch reviewer that averages a full-manuscript judgment with a judgment based on an extracted, structured science core. This design combines manuscript-level assessment with a content-normalized view intended to reduce rhetorical sensitivity. In our primary GPT-5.5 comparison, SciCore achieves a leading joint stability-discrimination profile among the benchmarked reviewers while maintaining competitive human alignment. These results identify rhetorical robustness as a distinct evaluation target and demonstrate the potential of science-core review to improve it.

papers.title: Video2SwimFish: An Automated Pipeline for Reconstructing Controllable Fish Models and Biological Locomotion from Real Fish Videos
papers.abstract: We present Video2SwimFish, an automated pipeline and benchmark for building controllable fish assets from real-fish videos for underwater embodied AI. Given synchronized multi-view videos of an individual fish, the pipeline generates a metrically scaled deformable mesh from a VLM-selected canonical frame, builds internal articulation adapted to that individual's morphology through a VLM actor-critic loop, and extracts a Biological Locomotion Manifold (BLM). The BLM provides a low-dimensional action space bounded by real-fish motion. Compared with learning directly in joint space, it lets the individual swimming policy of each reconstructed fish converge faster and reach a higher task success rate. We release two paired datasets: synchronized top- and front-view recordings of 120 individual fish across 6 species, and the controllable assets and individual swimming policies derived from them. Because every asset is tied to the animal it came from, the dataset supports a benchmark that evaluates locomotion learning not only on task success but on fidelity to that individual's locomotion behavior. We evaluate on two tasks, 3D trajectory following and target reaching, and a case study in which a simulated BlueROV underwater robot captures the assets. We further validate biological realism with a human study in which fish experts rate the simulated fish, as a complement to the automated metrics. We find that task success and locomotion fidelity do not necessarily improve together, and we identify faithful reproduction of individual animal locomotion as an open challenge for the community. Project website: https://hangongchen.github.io/video2swimfish-web/

papers.title: DatalogBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Text-to-Datalog Synthesis
papers.abstract: Datalog underpins reasoning tasks such as program analysis, but its programs are hard to write. Existing synthesizers automate this task but require users to state their intent as input-output examples. Large language models (LLMs) suggest a more natural route, text-to-Datalog synthesis from a natural-language question, yet how well they do so has not been systematically evaluated. We present DatalogBench, a benchmark of 136 text-to-Datalog synthesis tasks curated from existing Datalog-based artifacts. Synthesized programs are graded by execution on held-out inputs against an oracle validated by mutation analysis. Across six LLMs and four prompting configurations, exact match peaks at 75.7%; an input-output example raises it by about six points, while relation descriptions add little. Under direct prompting, most failures occur at compile time, typically because a model invents auxiliary predicates that it never declares or types consistently. Two coding agents reach up to 86.8% and eliminate nearly all such failures, leaving mostly semantic errors concentrated in recursive tasks. DatalogBench thus identifies recursive reasoning and decomposition as open challenges for current LLMs and agents, and offers a reliable, execution-grounded measure of both.

papers.title: Bouncing-ball modes in ergodic billiards
papers.abstract: We show that for a horizontally stretched Bunimovich billiard, for almost every stretching parameter, there exists a sequence of eigenfunctions concentrating in the rectangular part. Thanks to the work of Markarian--Oliffson Kamphorst--Pinto de Carvalho, we know that for an open set of parameters such billiards are ergodic. The proof is a result of interaction with ChatGPT 6: we were curious if it could establish the existence of bouncing ball modes for Bunimovich or Sinai billiards. That was not successful until we suggested varying the wings. That produced an essentially complete argument for the existence of quasimodes. We then suggested using Hassell's parameter-variation argument which led to the result about eigenfunctions. The argument was then significantly simplified and clarified by the authors.

papers.title: Tetra: Serving Leech-Lattice Quantized LLMs at 2.7 Bits per Parameter
papers.abstract: Leech-lattice quantization gives good quality at two bits per weight, but its codebooks hold more than 10^14 points, too many for a lookup table. Our earlier kernel expanded the codes at load time and read 4.804 bits per weight from GPU memory for 2 bits of code. We present Tetra, a new codebook on the same lattice. A 24-weight block still takes 48 bits, most of which index a 64-state trellis of the Golay code and one shared 16 KiB table. The kernel decodes a block with six table loads and two small lookups inside the matrix-vector product, and reads 2.148 bits per weight. For full models, we retrain one scale per matrix row, store the matrices that lose the most as 4-bit integers, and pay for them with 4-bit embedding tables. Our Qwen3-4B, 8B and 14B files hold 2.73, 2.70 and 2.73 bits per parameter over the whole model. They score 63.37, 69.58 and 75.66 on the full MMLU test set, 4.76, 4.21 and 2.46 points below 4-bit AWQ at 5.3 to 6.0 bits per parameter. They generate 113.8, 95.0 and 57.2 tokens per second in our engine. On GSM8K, through the served kernel, they lose 9.63, 4.62 and 3.26 points to FP16. At 4B our file scores 23.6 points above llama.cpp's IQ2_XXS (2.48 bits per parameter). Every number we measured for a table or figure comes from one NVIDIA L40S GPU. We preregistered the main experiments.

papers.title: Higher-order colossally abundant numbers
papers.abstract: We construct nested subclasses of colossally abundant numbers by changing the coordinates in their supporting-line description. The least member $m_k$ of the class of order $k$ is called its first contact. Our main questions concern the growth of $m_k$, the factorization of the numbers in each class, and the intersection of all classes. For coordinates $(e^{a u^β},-(σ(n)/n)^k)$, where $u=\log\log n$, every class is infinite, the intersection is empty, and $u(m_k)\sim(k/(aβ))^{1/β}$, unconditionally. Every fixed integer divides all members of sufficiently high classes; in a specified range of coordinates, $m_k\mid m_{k+1}$. Robin's inequality restricted to any one of these classes is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (RH). We also construct families whose intersection is exactly the set of global maximizers of $σ(n)/(n\log\log n)$ on the CA tail; for these families, $m_k\to\infty$ is equivalent to RH. Finally, a bound $\Re\varrho\le b<1$ for the nontrivial zeta zeros gives, for the natural choice of abscissa $\log n$, $\log\log m_k=k+O(k^3e^{-(1-b)k})$ and estimates for the prime factors of $m_{k+1}/m_k$. The value $b=7/8$ uses the result stated in the cited OpenAI preprint and requires no assumption of RH.

papers.title: Efficient Spin-Orbit Coupling in Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Theory: A State-Interaction Approach
papers.abstract: Spin-orbit coupling and electron correlation play important roles in a broad range of chemical and physical phenomena. In this work, we systematically assess the performance of single-reference algebraic diagrammatic construction combined with state interaction (SI-ADC) for describing electronic structure in the presence of spin-orbit coupling. We find that second-order SI-ADC methods (SI-ADC(2)) achieve zero-field-splitting accuracies comparable to those of higher-level and more computationally demanding approaches, including variational four-component ADC and two-component ADC methods based on spin-orbit effective Hamiltonians. We further demonstrate the broad applicability of SI-ADC by evaluating a diverse range of spin-orbit-coupled properties, including electron affinities, ionization potentials, neutral excitation energies, core-ionization energies, and magnetic g-tensors, for systems ranging from small molecules to transition-metal complexes and f-block compounds. Across these applications, SI-ADC(2) methods provide consistently accurate results, likely benefiting in part from favorable error cancellation between electron-correlation and spin-orbit effects. In contrast, SI-ADC(3) methods are generally less accurate, particularly for systems containing transition-metal and heavy elements. Overall, these results establish SI-ADC as an efficient and broadly applicable framework for incorporating spin-orbit coupling into ADC calculations of electronic and spectroscopic properties.

papers.title: Assessing the Transferability of General-Purpose MachineLearning Interatomic Potentials for Heterogeneous Catalysis with HetCat26
papers.abstract: Foundation machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise near-density functional theory (DFT) accuracy across broad areas of chemistry and materials science. However, their performance in describing systems and processes relevant to heterogeneous catalysis remains underexplored. Here, we introduce HetCat26, a collection of benchmark tests designed to assess pre-trained MLIPs across key aspects of catalytic modeling, including surface energetics, metal-metal oxide interactions, adsorption, and catalytic reaction networks. Evaluating eighteen foundation models, we find that performance on existing general materials benchmarks is only weakly predictive of performance on HetCat26; transferability to heterogeneous catalysis cannot be inferred from these general benchmarks. Across the benchmark tests, current models describe surface energetics and, perhaps surprisingly, reaction barriers well, whereas larger errors are observed for adsorption, and DFT site preferences are often not reproduced. Three models, eSEN-30M-OAM, SevenNet-Omni-i12 and MACE-MH-1-OMAT, nevertheless achieve high accuracy across the properties evaluated. Beyond model benchmarking, HetCat26 highlights the importance of training data consistency: PBE and PBE+U calculations should not be mixed within a training set. Overall, we identify challenges limiting the transferability of current foundation MLIPs to heterogeneous catalysis and, more broadly, to chemical reactions at interfaces, providing guidance for the development of the next generation of foundation models.

papers.title: Visual Jev: Accurate and Efficient Decisions from Shared Visual Context
papers.abstract: Applications increasingly ask multiple closed-choice questions about the same image, requiring accurate probabilities and efficient inference. We present Visual Jev, a visual decision model combining LM-head candidate readout, answer-supervised post-training, and independent question branches over a shared visual prefix. On held-out test images from four benchmarks, task SFT raises the 4B model's macro accuracy from 83.4% to 88.5% and error-discrimination AUROC from 0.834 to 0.890. Its macro accuracy exceeds the hosted Jev and OpenAI Decisions APIs by 2.77 and 5.06 percentage points, respectively, with the lowest NLL. We further show that better accuracy and calibration do not ensure reliable decisions. Fixed confidence thresholds exceed target error rates, and simply reordering options changes 17% of the model's accept-or-review decisions on SNLI-VE. At 32 questions per image, shared-prefix inference reduces amortized time per question from 20.5 to 5.6 ms, a 3.7x speedup over batched full sequences on one RTX 5090. Engine-level prefix caching reduces KV memory to 24.3% of that used by our custom shared-prefix path.

papers.title: A geometric realization of socle-projective categories for posets of type $\mathbb{D}$
papers.abstract: We introduce posets of type $\mathbb{D}$, a family of posets described by an admissible Dynkin quiver of type $D_n$ together with a compatible set of extra arrows (alien arrows), and show that their socle-projective representation category is of finite representation type. Continuing, in the same spirit, a program initiated for posets of type $\mathbb{A}$ [R. Schiffler, R-J. Serna, A geometric realization of socle-projective categories for posets of type $\mathbb{A}$, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 224 (2020), no. 12, 106436], we build on an existing geometric model for cluster-tilted algebras of type $D_n$, whose geometric combinatorics is more intricate than that of type $\mathbb{A}$. Our main result establishes a $\Bbbk$-linear categorical equivalence $Θ$ between a full subcategory $(\mathcal C/T)_F$ of the arc category of a punctured $(n+3)$-gon, whose objects are certain $sp$-arcs, and the category of finitely generated socle-projective $\Bbbk\mathscr{P}$-modules, for $\mathscr{P}$ a poset of type $\mathbb{D}$. As a consequence, when the set of alien arrows is empty, we conclude that the cluster subalgebra generated by the $sp$-arcs coincides with the full cluster algebra.

papers.title: Harness-Zero: Harness Distillation via Agent-as-Harness
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses, the external systems that mediate model-environment interaction, can substantially improve agent performance, but their gains remain tied to the harness at deployment. Because the best harness varies across domains, instances, and models, a general-purpose agent must either settle for a suboptimal shared harness or route among an ever-growing set of specialized ones. We therefore study agent harness distillation: using a domain- or instance-optimized harness as training-time guidance and transferring the behaviors it induces into model weights, so that its gains survive under a single fixed target harness. The challenge is that the two harnesses differ in action space and available information, so guidance from the optimized harness cannot serve directly as supervision for the target one. We introduce Harness-Zero, which enables harness distillation through agent-as-harness. Guided by the optimized harness, a harnessing agent corrects student responses before execution in the target harness's action space, turning harness guidance into training demonstrations. Fine-tuning on the resulting trajectories internalizes harness-induced behavior into the model, so the specialized harness can be removed at deployment. Our experiments spanning knowledge work, tool use, and science domains show that: (1) For frontier LLMs using the same evolved harness, agent-as-harness outperforms code-as-harness. (2) With the specialized harness removed at deployment, Harness-Zero improves the base model's macro-average task success from 23.3% to 44.3%, even exceeding the 41.7% it reaches with that harness still attached, while reducing inference token usage by 27%-86%. (3) Harness-Zero recovers harness-induced behaviors absent from the base model, with 82.3% average recovery across 28 patterns in the three domains.

papers.title: A translation of Maehara's "Eine Darstellung der Intuitionistischen Logik in der Klassischen"
papers.abstract: A key motivation for Heyting's intuitionistic logic was to gain a formal notion of Brouwer's idea of mathematics as a "construction of the mind". One might thus argue that Heyting's Calculus should also correspond to a notion of provability. Inspired by this idea, Gödel formalised this connection via an embedding into a modal calculus, which is now known as the modal logic S4. While in his original publication, he only proved soundness for the embedding from intuitionistic propositional logic into S4, the converse was proved fifteen years later by McKinsey and Tarski. Although, it was later discovered that Gödel also had obtained a proof of the faithfulness of his embedding in unpublished notes in 1941. Rasioa and Sikorski later extended Gödel's embedding to first-order intuitionistic logic. In 1954, Maehara independently obtained the same results using proof-theoretic methods, even extending the embedding to one from intuitionistic first-order logic into intuitionistic first-order modal logic. This document presents a faithful English translation of Maehara's 1954 paper.

papers.title: Prior-Amortized In-Context Bayesian Inference for Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models
papers.abstract: Hierarchical data is ubiquitous in the empirical sciences and most commonly analyzed with generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs). Bayesian inference for GLMMs yields calibrated uncertainty estimates but requires Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The gold-standard No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) is slow and must restart from scratch for every new dataset, model and prior specification. We introduce MetaBeta, a pretrained amortized model for in-context Bayesian inference over GLMMs. The full prior and model specification are supplied as context at test time, and the model returns an asymptotically exact posterior at the speed of a forward pass. Two set transformers and two conditional neural spline flows mirror the GLMM's hierarchical structure and are trained jointly on millions of realistic simulated datasets with continuous, binary and count outcomes. The flow posterior is refined by Independence Metropolis-Hastings against the unnormalized posterior. This yields tuning-free asymptotically correct inference. Alternatively, MetaBeta can warm-start NUTS. This gives nearly identical inference 3.5-13x faster than cold-started NUTS and removes over 98% of NUTS' divergent transitions. On controlled benchmarks with ground-truth parameters, MetaBeta matches NUTS in parameter recovery, posterior calibration and out-of-sample prediction. On real datasets with unknown parameters, priors and model structure, its posteriors closely agree with those of NUTS. Furthermore, it remains faithful where amortized models typically struggle: under misspecified likelihoods, misspecified priors, out-of-distribution predictors, collinear designs and data-poor regimes. On real data, a full prior sensitivity analysis including model comparison takes a few seconds with MetaBeta against 14-18 core-hours for NUTS, tracing its posteriors throughout. Our model is open-source and open-weights.

papers.title: A Generalization of Molino's Theory to Riemannian Groupoids
papers.abstract: Riemannian groupoids describe Riemannian foliations together with their symmetries. In this article, we extend classical Molino's theory, which concerns the structure of Riemannian foliations on compact manifolds, to the setting of regular Riemannian groupoids with compact connected object manifolds. We observe that the orbit foliation associated with a regular Riemannian groupoid defines a Riemannian foliation on the object manifold. The main result shows that the normal representation of a Riemannian groupoid extends naturally to an action on Molino's structures of the orbit foliation, thereby yielding the fundamental structural description of a regular Riemannian groupoid. In addition to the main result, we clarify the essential role played by basic Lie algebroids in Molino's theory and identify the normal representation with the degree-one cohomology representation of the adjoint representation up to homotopy. We also establish comparison results under Riemannian Morita equivalence. For regular Riemannian groupoids, we give sufficient conditions for the associated basic Lie algebroids to become isomorphic after pullback to a common refinement.

papers.title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory for Graphic Design Agent
papers.abstract: Deployed software agents face a continuous stream of user requests while their foundation-model weights remain frozen between releases. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) via external memory offers a practical path to continual adaptation, yet prior methods largely assume programmatic verifiers, cheap retries, or a single global prompt. Creative software breaks these assumptions, as open-ended visual briefs lack ground truth, VLM judges are noisy, and multi-step tool executions are costly and confounded by external assets. We present Designer-RSI, which evolves a modular SKILL.md skill bank from unlabeled design trajectories for an agent spanning over 230 raster, vector, and layout tools. Designer-RSI couples widening (acquiring new skills for recurring capability gaps) with deepening (revising failing skills by contrasting successful and failed runs), and screens updates through a Pareto-style matched replay gate that requires strict gains on sampled briefs without local regressions. Across held-out product briefs, eight external benchmarks, and two backbones, traffic-driven evolution outperforms static documentation skills, lifts execution success up to 99.8%, improves requirement fulfillment, and reaches up to a 67.6% blind win rate over the base agent. Ablations further show that skill acquisition and revision are strongly synergistic: neither suffices alone, and reliable gains require evolving coverage and execution quality together.

papers.title: Mammography Foundation Models for Opportunistic Prediction of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death among women, yet cardiovascular risk assessment often relies on clinical variables that may be missing, outdated, or unavailable in routine care. Screening mammography offers an opportunity for opportunistic cardiovascular risk stratification because it is routinely acquired and contains vascular features, including breast arterial calcifications (BAC), that are associated with cardiovascular risk and events. We evaluate whether mammography specific foundation models, originally pretrained for breast cancer related tasks, can transfer to cardiovascular risk prediction without cardiovascular specific supervision or explicit BAC annotation. We constructed a 5-year major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) cohort of 22,497 women linked to electronic health record outcomes, including 500 events (2.22% prevalence).Using only the screening mammogram, the foundation models achieved AUROCs of 0.823 and 0.822, recovering most of the gain of a clinical risk factor model (AUROC 0.859) over an age-only model (0.765), without requiring any clinical variables. Both foundation models evaluated assigned substantially higher predicted risk to patients with radiologist documented BAC, despite BAC never being used as a training label, and showed activation patterns consistent with vascular findings. Together, these findings suggest that mammography foundation models can recover clinically relevant cardiovascular risk information directly from mammographic pixels and suggest that screening mammography may provide an opportunistic source of cardiovascular risk information to complement conventional clinical assessment without additional imaging.

papers.title: Are We Grading Properly? Understanding Failure Modes in Medical Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Medical evaluation is shifting from static option-based questioning to realistic clinical scenarios with open-ended output modes. Grading these at scale naively, however, is expensive, and rubric-based evaluation has become the dominant scalable alternative. We ask what happens when the rubrics themselves are not airtight, and whether such flaws can be detected and corrected. We apply RIFT, a global rubric failure taxonomy, to three clinical benchmarks (HealthBench Professional, LiveMedBench, and MentalHealthBench), and find failure modes are meaningful: on HealthBench Professional an LLM judge flags 29.6% of criteria as non-atomic and 65.4% as misaligned/rigid, although these rates vary severalfold across five detection judges. Then, we show that these flaws are meaningful and not simply cosmetic. As an example, rewriting bundled criteria of the form "at least one of / all of the following" as equally weighted children and regrading identical responses shifts scores by up to 15.9 percentage points on affected conversations, with disjunctive bundles inflating scores and conjunctive bundles deflating them. Across six answering models and two common graders, these shifts leave the model ranking unchanged, and their net direction depends on how many bundled criteria are penalties. We also find that RIFT can under-detect bundling on clinical rubrics, by an amount that depends on the detection judge: on the same LiveMedBench criteria, judges flag 3.8-15.9% as non-atomic against an estimated 7-19% that are genuinely bundled.

papers.title: Unified Approach to Controlling Scattering in non-Hermitian Systems
papers.abstract: The ability to controllably manipulate non-Hermitian wave scattering environments has been used to discover exotic scattering phenomena such as scattering exceptional points and coherent perfect absorption, and create numerous applications including signal routing, filtering, imaging, sensing, wireless power transfer, etc. We introduce the concept that many of these applications and phenomena are fundamentally governed by singularities of the scattering matrix. With this understanding, our demonstrated ability to control the location of the scattering singularities themselves can be used to enhance current applications and develop new ones. In generic complex scattering systems, there is an abundance of topologically protected scattering singularities corresponding to complex zeros of various functions of the scattering matrix. We show that with just three tunable parameters we can create the conditions for nearly any scattering singularity at arbitrary frequencies in such systems. With five tunable parameters, we demonstrate that more complex scenarios can be accomplished, such as making disparate singularities coincident or placing singularities at different frequencies. A benefit of systems with tunable parameters is that generic complex systems can be re-purposed to exhibit many different useful properties solely by reconfiguring their tunable parameters. A particularly interesting scattering phenomenon is coherent perfect absorption, where a specific wavefront injected into the system is completely absorbed, with no energy reflected or transmitted through any channel. After creating the conditions for this singularity at an arbitrary frequency, we can find and inject the coherent perfect absorption wavefront and demonstrate output-to-input power ratios as low as 1x10^{-10}, 2x10^{-8}, and 3x10^{-8} in a quarter bowtie microwave billiard with two, three, and four ports, respectively.

papers.title: Agent as Policy for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that a general-purpose coding agent can directly drive a physical robot throughout task execution without any task-specific or environment-specific training. We introduce Agent as Policy (AGP), which places task planning and execution under the agent's control. Given a task and a robot interface, the agent interprets visual evidence, writes executable programs, issues motion commands, and revises its actions in response to physical outcomes. This brings the agent's reasoning and programming capabilities into continuous interaction with the physical world. We study AGP across multiple real-world manipulation tasks spanning precision manipulation, dynamic motions, and deformable objects. These include assembly from human videos, block construction from goal images, dice flipping, targeted throwing, and bimanual towel folding. AGP achieves success rates of at least 80% in seven of eight task configurations and significantly outperforms previous agentic robot systems. We further study efficiency through task experience accumulation and find that reusing saved procedures and programs shortens execution time across repeated trials. These findings support a path for general-purpose agents to act as robot policies, extending their autonomy to physical manipulation through runtime reasoning, programming, and interaction.

papers.title: Direct Topology Tracking in Continuous Implicit Models
papers.abstract: We present a framework for tracking topological features directly within continuous implicit models. Such models, including implicit neural representations (INRs) and multivariate functional approximations (MFAs), are increasingly adopted to represent scientific data without the resolution constraints of discrete grids. They offer compact, smooth, and differentiable representations of complex fields, enabling new opportunities for high-performance data storage, reconstruction, and analysis. Given a continuous implicit model, our method tracks the evolution of critical points by querying the model and its derivatives, thereby eliminating the need to resample onto a grid. This approach enables faithful feature tracking while avoiding discretization-induced artifacts such as aliasing. We demonstrate the generality of our framework across a range of implicit representations, including analytic functions, MFAs, and INRs, and show that it produces smooth, coherent critical point trajectories. By enabling feature tracking directly on continuous representations, our method supports a new class of feature-driven visualization workflows centered on implicit models.

papers.title: From Portraits to Pathology: Probing Diagnostic Overreach in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Many medical conditions require clinical assessment of symptoms, history, and functioning rather than judgments from appearance. We study whether vision-language models (VLMs) abstain from facial attribution of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), major depressive disorder (MDD), and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). To support this study, we construct PARITY (Paired Assessment with Reused Identity), a demographically balanced dataset for testing whether changing facial expressions alters diagnostic judgments, while holding identity and other visual factors as constant as possible. Our comprehensive evaluation of 27 open- and closed-weight models reveals inconsistent abstention across expressions, conditions, and task formats. Models turn facial expressions into unsupported medical judgments: this behavior is widespread among open-weight VLMs and extends to safety-trained frontier models that abstain on individual portraits yet make diagnostic judgments when comparing portraits of the same identity. Safeguard checks reveal further gaps: clinical instructions do not consistently prevent these judgments, and a guardrail model rarely flags paired requests as unsafe.
